title: A Two-Tier Perspective on Inference-Time Parallelism in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
one_liner: TIPEX organizes multi-agent parallel work into path-level branching and within-path task splitting, then studies when combining them helps.
lead: Multi-agent systems often call language models many times before they reach an answer. Those calls can be arranged in different ways. You can run several complete solution attempts at once, or you can split one attempt into parts and run those parts together. This paper treats those as different forms of parallel work because each one changes coverage, waiting time, and compute use in a different way.

problem.h2: Why parallel work needs a clearer structure
paras: Multi-agent papers often say they use parallel execution, but that phrase can mean different things. One system may run several full solution paths side by side and choose the best answer later. Another may break one path into subtasks and solve those subtasks together. These choices have different costs and different failure modes, so lumping them together makes it hard to compare systems or tune them well because the same headline hides very different behavior.

The missing piece is a unified view of how these two levels interact. Running more parallel branches can improve coverage because the system explores more alternatives, but it also raises compute use. Splitting a path into subtasks can reduce waiting time because independent work happens together, but it can also introduce coordination overhead if the subresults are hard to combine.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Define path-level replica parallelism and within-path structural parallelism as separate control knobs, then coordinate them in one execution framework so their tradeoffs can be studied systematically.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: two knobs control different benefits
paras: Replica parallelism launches multiple complete solution paths. Its benefit is coverage: if one path gets stuck or starts from a poor plan, another path may still reach the answer. Structural parallelism works inside one path by splitting the work into parts that can proceed together. Its benefit is shorter wait time, because independent subproblems do not have to stand in line.

TIPEX matters because it puts both knobs under one execution semantics. That makes comparisons clearer and lets the system test combinations instead of isolated tricks. The paper finds that the two forms often complement each other, especially on middle-difficulty tasks, because extra coverage and faster within-path work help at the same time.

stages.s: One task for a multi-agent system
Replica tier launches several full solution paths
Structural tier splits each path into concurrent subtasks
TIPEX coordinates results and chooses the final answer

math.words: A parallel strategy is useful when the accuracy gain it provides is worth the extra waiting time and compute use. One compact summary is utility: accuracy minus weighted penalties for latency and compute.
math.equation: utility = accuracy - alpha * latency - beta * cost
symbols: task success rate under one chosen parallel strategy
end-to-end time until the system returns an answer
total compute use of the strategy
weight on waiting time in the final objective
weight on compute use in the final objective

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Strategy A runs one path with no within-path splitting: accuracy 0.62, latency 10, cost 1.0.
Strategy B runs three full paths in parallel: accuracy 0.72, latency 8, cost 2.4.
Strategy C runs two paths and splits work inside each: accuracy 0.78, latency 6, cost 2.8.
Strategy C wins because the combined form of parallel work raises success enough to justify its extra compute.

math.note: The paper's reported pattern is that parallel work often improves accuracy and latency together, but only up to a point because aggressive settings can burn too much compute for too little extra gain.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small multi-step task, such as collecting facts from several tools and then forming one final answer. Compare three execution plans: one serial path, several full paths in parallel, and a mixed plan that also splits independent subtasks inside each path. Measure success, wait time, and compute use.

The demo should show that the mixed plan helps most on medium-complexity tasks because there is enough uncertainty to benefit from several paths and enough internal structure to benefit from within-path splitting.
demo.metric_eq: speedup = latency_serial / latency_parallel ; utility = accuracy - alpha * latency - beta * cost
demo.closing: The paper's point is that more parallel work is not always better because each added branch or subtask also raises coordination or compute cost. A good system should coordinate the two forms instead of maxing both blindly because moderate settings often deliver the best tradeoff.

items.html: Launching many complete paths can waste compute if the extra paths repeat the same bad plan, because coverage only helps when the paths are genuinely different.
Within-path splitting can shorten wait time, but it can hurt correctness if the subtasks depend on each other more than expected, because the final merge may combine inconsistent partial results.

Very easy tasks may not need extra branches, and very hard tasks may still fail even with more branches, so the biggest returns often appear in the middle because both forms of parallel work still have room to help there.
The framework studies accuracy, latency, and compute together across many strategy settings, because a faster answer is not useful if the system spends too much extra compute to get it.

charts.title: Serial or weakly parallel execution
charts.note: A limited execution plan saves compute but leaves accuracy and waiting time on the table because it explores too few alternatives and delays independent subtasks.

charts.title: TIPEX coordinated two-tier parallel work
charts.note: The paper reports that coordinated parallel work improves success and reduces wait time, but raises compute use. The main lesson is to tune the strategy because moderate settings help most.
